summary: Proposes organizing internet host names into hierarchical name domains, so that every host does not need to be listed in every table. It aims to fit existing mail systems and scale to thousands of hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo proposes dividing computer names into domains and using forwarders to find hosts in other domains. It gives a structured mailbox form and discusses how messages could move between domains.

questions: what is the internet mailbox name syntax
subtitle: A proposed domain structure for Internet host names and mail forwarding.

tldr.problem: Keeping every Internet host in every other host's name-address table was becoming impractical.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal groups hosts into name domains, gives each domain forwarders, and uses mailbox names in the form user.host@domain.
tldr.outcome: The memo presents a scheme intended to fit existing mail systems and grow to thousands of hosts, and says it is meant to stimulate discussion.

sections.title: Why Divide Name Tables
sections.content:
The memo argues that it would not be practical for every Internet host to list every other host in its name-address table. It cites more than four hundred names and nicknames in the combined ARPANET-DCNET tables as already awkward to manage.

It proposes hierarchical name-space partitioning that the author believed could work with known mail systems and scale to thousands of hosts. The closing section says the memorandum is intended to stimulate discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: One list of every host becomes difficult to maintain as the network grows. This memo proposes dividing the names into domains.

sections.title: Domains, Forwarders, and Mailbox Names
sections.content:
A name domain represents a group such as an institution. Each domain has one or more mail forwarder processes that keep name-address tables for hosts in that domain and at least one forwarder in each other domain. A host may belong to several domains, and the proposal assumes a single-level domain structure.

The general mailbox form is <user>.<host>@<domain>. Hosts in one domain may use a different form if forwarders can translate it and it does not conflict with the general form. Shorter names may work locally but be ambiguous elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain's forwarders know its hosts and how to reach other domains. A full mailbox name identifies the person, their host, and the domain.

sections.title: Mail Routes, Relays, and Header Changes
sections.content:
The proposal expects most mail to travel directly from sender to recipient. A relay can store a message for later transmission when the hosts are not available together, lack translation resources, cannot connect directly, or use incompatible lower-level transports. Every forwarder is a relay, but not every relay is a forwarder.

The sender specifies a relay sequence in the source route. Complete names are needed when a relay serves more than one domain. The memo advises avoiding edits to the RFC 733 header; where needed, edits should occur when mail first enters the Internet mail system.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail can go directly to its destination or pass through relays. Full domain names help relays route it without confusing similar host names.
